transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining. As you know, Harbor Point Properties has submitted a restructuring proposal requesting a 12-month maturity extension, a waiver of the current financial covenant, and release of $900,000 of equipment collateral on our $8 million term loan. Before I can record any final terms, I need each of you to walk through your findings — risk, relationship coverage, legal, and collateral management. Jonas, I'll also need your covenant-testing findings with the applicable workout policy cited. Per our standard process, the applicable treatment depends on the current covenant test and supporting policy materials, so we can't simply finalize from the borrower's requested terms. Let's get started — who would like to begin?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I'll go ahead and start with the covenant-testing findings. I reviewed the file this week, and I need to flag a couple of important points before we proceed. However, I want to be transparent — I have not yet attached the testing file to the committee package, so I'll need to make sure that gets circulated. Let me walk through what I've found so the group has the full picture.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: I'd like to jump in with a relationship update before we go further. This morning I received a signed term sheet from Harbor Point committing the owners to inject exactly $1,200,000 of new equity at restructuring closing. This commitment has not yet been entered in the relationship system, so I want to make sure the committee is aware of it now, as it may be relevant to the restructuring decision.

transcript.text: I need to raise a legal issue before we go further. While reviewing the intercreditor agreement this week, I confirmed that the senior lender must give written consent before any equipment collateral is released. That consent has not yet been requested. This means the borrower's request to release $900,000 of equipment collateral cannot proceed until we obtain that written consent from the senior lender.

transcript.text: I completed a collateral review yesterday, and the findings are significant. Receivables are the weakest and most volatile part of the collateral package. Under our collateral policy, this means a weekly borrowing-base certificate will be required throughout any extension period. I should also note that I have not yet updated the monitoring schedule to reflect this requirement, so that will need to be done before any restructuring is finalized.

Jonas, you mentioned covenant-testing findings but noted the testing file hasn't been circulated yet — I'll need that attached to the committee package and the applicable workout policy cited before I can record final terms, since the treatment depends on the current covenant test and supporting policy materials. Nadia, the weekly borrowing-base certificate requirement for receivables is noted, and the monitoring schedule will need to be updated before finalization. Before I can settle on terms, Jonas, I still need your full covenant-testing findings with the policy citation. Can you walk us through those now?

transcript.text: I need to share my full covenant-testing findings with the committee. Here's what I found: Harbor Point's leverage is 0.3x above the permitted level. Under the applicable workout policy, a covenant waiver is allowed only with a 9-month extension — not the 12 months the borrower requested — and requires a monthly leverage certificate throughout the extension period. I'll make sure the testing file is attached to the committee package so everyone has the supporting documentation.

transcript.text: Thank you, Jonas. From a legal perspective, the covenant-testing findings are clear — the policy caps the extension at 9 months and requires a monthly leverage certificate, which is shorter than the borrower's requested 12 months. I'd note that the borrower's proposal as submitted cannot be finalized as-is for multiple legal reasons: first, the 12-month extension exceeds what the workout policy permits given the 0.3x leverage breach; second, the equipment collateral release requires senior lender written consent that has not yet been requested; and third, the new equity injection commitment Mei flagged will need to be properly documented in the loan file. Elena, when you record the final terms, I'd recommend they reflect the 9-month extension cap, the monthly leverage certificate requirement, the weekly borrowing-base certificate Nadia identified, and a condition that no equipment collateral is released until we have the senior lender's written consent on file. I'll prepare the consent request to the senior lender so we can move that forward in parallel.

transcript.text: Thank you, Rafael. From a collateral management perspective, I can confirm that the weekly borrowing-base certificate requirement I identified is directly tied to the volatility in the receivables portion of the package, and it will need to run concurrently with Jonas's monthly leverage certificate throughout the extension period. I'll update the monitoring schedule to reflect both the weekly borrowing-base certificate and the 9-month extension cap once Elena records the final terms. One thing I want to flag for Elena: the borrower's request to release $900,000 of equipment collateral would effectively remove a portion of the collateral package at a time when receivables — already the weakest component — are showing significant volatility. Even if the senior lender's written consent is obtained per Rafael's point, I'd recommend the committee carefully weigh whether releasing equipment collateral is prudent given the receivables findings. I'm comfortable with the 9-month extension cap, the monthly leverage certificate, and the weekly borrowing-base certificate as the collateral monitoring framework for any finalized terms.
